title: Fibonacci phyllotaxis: one parastichy pair entails all lower pairs
look_for_in_this_kingdom: surveys of parastichy numbers and divergence angles across species and organ types (cones, sunflower heads, cacti, succulents, shoots); meristem imaging datasets; non-Fibonacci and anomalous cases too
variables_needed: parastichy pair (m, n) or divergence angle per organism
leaves or organs per turn of the genetic spiral
species and organ (cone, capitulum, shoot, rosette)

claims.label: One Fibonacci parastichy pair necessarily entails all the lower pairs
claims.statement: Following Tait, if a single genetic spiral exists and one pair of parastichy numbers from the series 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… is present, all the lower pairs of the series are necessarily present in the same system.
claims.quote: These are the very series which we have found to be common, or normal; and so far as our investigation has yet gone, it has proved to us that, if one of these exists, it entails, _ipso facto_, the presence of the rest.

claims.label: Most phyllotaxis has between two and three leaves per turn of the genetic spiral
claims.statement: The prevalence of Fibonacci parastichy numbers arises because in the great majority of fir-cones and other phyllotactic systems there are more than two but fewer than three leaves in one turn of the genetic spiral (t = 2); other observed series correspond to t = 3, 4, 5.
claims.quote: And, determined in this manner, it is found in the great majority of cases, in fir-cones and a host of other examples of phyllotaxis, that _t_ = 2.

other_kingdoms_hint.animals: spiral or Fibonacci arrangements outside plants (coral polyps, sponge or bryozoan zooids, feather and scale placement, Volvox-like colonies); say plainly when the animal side is thin
other_kingdoms_hint.fossils: leaf cushions and scars (Lepidodendron, Sigillaria, Calamites), fossil cones, cycadeoids, crinoid and echinoderm plate spirals; counts of parastichies from fossil specimens
